title: How does dividing by primes break a number into primes?
description: One hundred and five and thirty are broken into primes by dividing by a prime again and again, writing each answer below. The divisors on the left and the last number are collected into the prime factorisation. Keeko's doubt, dividing by six, is tested because six is not a prime.
teaching_notes: One idea: divide by a prime, write the answer below, and stop when the number left is prime. Watch for students who divide by a composite number such as six.

source: Use the division method to find the prime factorisation of 1
video_script.why: The child can split numbers into trees but has not yet used repeated division by primes as a neat method.
video_script.substitution: Divide by a prime, write the answer below, and repeat until the number left is itself prime.
video_script.anchor: Two columns of repeated division, one for one hundred and five and one for thirty, with the primes written on the left.
video_script.wrong_answer: six is one of the primes
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko divides thirty by six to get five and says six is one of the primes. But six is two times three, so six is not a prime at all.
video_script.payoff_line: One hundred and five is three times five times seven.

final_answer.spoken: one hundred and five is three times five times seven, and thirty is two times three times five

maths_rules: Division method: divide by a prime, write the answer below, repeat until the number left is prime.
105 / 3 = 35; 35 / 5 = 7; 7 is prime, so stop. The divisors and the last number are 3, 5, 7.
30 / 2 = 15; 15 / 3 = 5; 5 is prime, so stop. The divisors and the last number are 2, 3, 5.
Slip: 30 / 6 = 5, but 6 = 2 x 3 is not prime, so dividing by 6 does not give primes.
video_script.design: One idea: divide by a prime each time and stop at a prime. Assumes the child knows primes. Wrong idea: dividing by six. The two columns stay on the board all video.
